html:
A famine in Finland, Estonia, Livonia and northern Sweden from 1695 to 1697, caused by years of cold weather and failed harvests. Finland, then part of the Swedish kingdom, lost roughly a quarter to a third of its people.

The 1690s were among the coldest years of the Little Ice Age. Early frosts and wet summers destroyed the rye and barley in the north. Poor roads and slow government meant grain could not be moved fast, and people ate bark bread and grass. Hunger brought typhus and dysentery, and many died while wandering in search of food. Estonia lost perhaps a fifth of its people.

The same cold years brought famine to Scotland and France. The Baltic famine weakened Sweden just before the Great Northern War began in 1700, which ended Swedish power in the region and moved Estonia and Livonia to Peter the Great's Russia.
